name: difftastic
why: Syntax-aware diffing parses code into trees, a clever transform, though well known among diff tool users.

brief.what_it_is: Difftastic is a command-line diff tool, installed as the executable difft, that compares two files by their syntax rather than line by line. It parses each file into a syntax tree using tree-sitter, then reports what actually changed, so an inner expression that is merely wrapped or reformatted is not shown as a deleted and re-added line. It takes two files (or a single file containing git merge conflict markers) and prints a human-readable diff with real line numbers from both files. It supports over 30 programming languages and several file formats such as HCL, HTML, JSON and YAML; unrecognised extensions fall back to a line-oriented diff with word highlighting.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames it around the problem that a line-oriented diff misleads people: a reformatter splitting code across lines, or a wrapper added around an expression, produces noisy diffs that hide what really changed. The homepage says it produces accurate diffs that are easier for humans to read.
brief.how_it_works: Files are parsed with tree-sitter into syntax trees, and the comparison is treated as a graph problem solved with Dijkstra's algorithm. The README says that when parse errors are found it falls back to a line-oriented diff by default, to avoid claiming two syntactically different files are the same; a DFT_PARSE_ERROR_LIMIT environment variable can allow a few parse errors. The author's blog post and the manual's internals section describe the design.

commands_seen.context: Sets an environment variable so difftastic tolerates up to 20 parse errors before falling back to a line-oriented diff; the README suggests this for C++ and similar files.
Basic usage: diffs two C files structurally, shown alongside the parse-error-limit example.
Passing a single file containing merge conflict markers; difftastic builds the two conflicting versions and diffs those (added in version 0.50).
Diffing JSON with keys sorted first, so reordered keys do not show as changes, since difftastic always treats order as significant.
Checks whether two files have the same AST without computing a diff; exit code 0 means no syntactic changes, 1 means changes were found.
Disables ANSI bright colours for users of Solarized and similar themes where bright colours render as grey.

brief.install_notes: The homepage links to an Install page and the README points to the manual's installation section for instructions; I did not open those pages, so beyond the brew install named in the catalogue entry I have no specific steps. The README mentions a crates.io package (difftastic) and says it integrates with git via configuration instructions in the manual, and with mercurial as well. No hardware, account, or runtime requirements were visible in the pages I read.
brief.standout: Structural diffing is a well-known idea among diff tool users, but difftastic is notable for treating the problem as a shortest-path search over a graph, and for choosing to fall back to a line diff on parse errors rather than risk declaring different files equal. It also diffs merge-conflict files directly and offers a fast AST-equality check with a useful exit code.
brief.status: Unknown from the pages I read. The README references a release (version 0.50, dated 2023-08-16) and a crates.io badge, and the project has a Codecov badge and an active-looking manual, but I did not see a latest release date or last commit date, so I cannot confirm current maintenance.
brief.caveats: The README lists known issues: it scales relatively poorly on files with many changes and can use a lot of memory; its side-by-side display can be confusing; and it has regular releases that fix crashes. It is not a patch generator (use diff for patches) and does not do merges (the README points to mergiraf for AST merging). It is order-sensitive, so set(1, 2) and set(2, 1) show as changed. Parse errors cause fallback to a line diff, and preprocessor-dependent languages like C++ can hit this. Some terminal themes such as Solarized render the bright colours grey unless DFT_BACKGROUND=light is set. The author notes the project is young and does not integrate with every tool. Licence is MIT, with vendored tree-sitter parsers under MIT or Apache licences.
quotes: Difftastic is a structural diff tool that compares files based on their syntax.

entry.title: difftastic
entry.tldr: A diff tool that parses code into syntax trees and shows what actually changed, so reformatting and wrapping stop looking like rewrites.
entry.deeper_look:
Difftastic installs one executable, `difft`. Give it two files and it parses each with tree-sitter into a syntax tree, then compares the trees instead of the lines. It handles over 30 programming languages plus formats like HCL, HTML, JSON and YAML. Unrecognised extensions fall back to a line-oriented diff with word highlighting.

The problem it targets is that line diffs mislead. A reformatter that splits an expression across several lines, or a wrapper added around an existing expression, produces a noisy diff that hides the real change. In the README's words: "Difftastic is not line-oriented. If you reformat your code and it's now split over multiple lines, difftastic will show you what's actually changed."

The idea underneath is that comparing two trees can be treated as a graph problem. The comparison becomes a shortest-path search, solved with Dijkstra's algorithm, over the possible ways to turn one tree into the other. The author's blog post and the manual's internals section describe the design.

One design choice stands out. When it hits parse errors, it falls back to a line diff by default, to avoid claiming two syntactically different files are the same. You can loosen that with the `DFT_PARSE_ERROR_LIMIT` environment variable. It can also take a single file containing git merge conflict markers, rebuild the two sides and diff those.

try_this.what_happens: Diffs two C files structurally and prints the changes with real line numbers from both files.
Checks whether the two files have the same syntax tree without printing a diff. Exit code 0 means no syntactic changes, 1 means changes were found.
Takes one file containing merge conflict markers, builds the two conflicting versions and diffs them (needs version 0.50 or later).

entry.whats_unique: It treats diffing as a shortest-path search over syntax trees, and it prefers a plain line diff to the risk of calling different files equal after a parse error. It can also diff conflict-marked files directly.
entry.caveats: The README says it scales poorly on files with many changes and can use a lot of memory, it is order-sensitive so set(1, 2) and set(2, 1) show as changed, and it is not a patch generator or a merge tool.
